c_heronarch.text: A grey heron stands in the mud as still as a fence post. It has been here since breakfast. It will be here at tea.

c_moolet.text: This one is called Daisy. Every cow on this farm is called Daisy. It saves time.

then.text: The pods are grand. Somebody's got their dorsal fins all catalogued, you know. Each one's notched different, like a fingerprint.
You saw him off? Dónal and his speedboat? Fair play to you. Here, take these. And thank you, from me and from about a hundred and forty dolphins.
Go easy, look, don't chase, let them come to you. That's the whole of dolphin watching.
Three pods: off the mud east of here, down by the crossing, and off Foynes on the far shore. Then if you see a fella in a speedboat buzzing them, Dónal, have a word. A firm word.

else.text: Dia dhuit! I run the dolphin watch. The Shannon's got its own dolphins, did you know? Over a hundred, here all year, the only resident pod in Ireland.
I'm counting them for the survey. Will you spot three pods for me? Off the mud east of the slip, by the crossing, and off Foynes. Wade out if you've the legs for it, but don't crowd them.

then.text: The dolphin rolls, blows a fine spray, and pretends it hasn't seen you. It has.
A fin, then another, then a whole family arcing through the water off the Bunratty mud. You note the pod for Skipper Gráinne's survey.

else.text: A bottlenose dolphin surfaces with a pfff and looks you over. It's a lot bigger than it looks from the road.

then.text: I've taken up kayaking. It's very quiet. I hate it. The dolphins love it.
Dónal ties up his speedboat. The dolphins, somewhere out on the channel, carry on regardless.

else.text: Dolphins? Haven't seen any. Have you looked?
Dolphins? Haven't seen any. Have you looked?
Lovely day for a blast down the estuary. Vroom.

then.text: Float it, mind. Never stir an Irish coffee. You drink the hot through the cold. That's the magic.

else.text: Cream for the Foynes coffee? Of course. Golden Vale cream, the richest grass in Ireland goes into that.
Lightly whipped, so it'll float. Not stiff. Stiff cream sits on top like a hat.
You've got a jug of cream for the chef at Foynes.
This is the Golden Vale, or the edge of it, the best dairy land in Ireland. Limestone under the grass, rain on top. The cows are very pleased with themselves.
Half the butter on Irish tables starts with cows like these. The other half's lying.

then.text: I'll be there, tuned and fed. The harp's the national symbol, you know. It's on the coins and the passports. And the stout, which I don't mention at the banquet.

else.text: Play for the banquet tonight? I will, of course. The Butler always forgets to ask till the soup's on.
Turlough O'Carolan wrote two hundred tunes for the big houses, and he was blind from the age of eighteen. I play his Planxty for the toast.
Síle the harpist will play at the banquet.
The wire-strung harp is older in Ireland than anyone can say for sure. I play gut strings. My great-great-grandmother would have something to say about that.

ferry_north.text: Killimer to Tarbert, twenty minutes, all aboard. The dolphins race us most days.

ferry_south.text: Tarbert to Killimer, back over to Clare. Mind the step, it's wet. It's always wet.

est_plane_spotter.text: Shannon's runway is over three kilometres long. It was a NASA emergency landing site for the Space Shuttle, you know. It never came. I waited anyway.
Charles Lindbergh flew in to look at Foynes before the war. Everybody who was anybody came through here on the way to New York.

est_folk_guide.text: Those cottages are Clare and Limerick farmhouses, saved and moved here stone by stone. The half-door keeps the hens out and lets the news in.
The thatch is reed and straw. A good thatch lasts twenty years if the jackdaws behave. They don't.

est_mudlarker.text: The estuary mud's the richest larder in Ireland at low tide. Dunlin, godwits, curlew, lapwing, thousands of them, every winter.
It's a Special Protection Area for the birds and a Special Area of Conservation for the dolphins. Very special, all round.

est_foynes_local.text: My granny served tea to film stars off the flying boats. Maureen O'Hara's husband flew them, you know. Charles Blair. She ran the museum's honour after, God rest her.
In the war, Ireland was neutral, so Foynes had passengers from both sides through the same lounge. My granny said the tea was strictly neutral too.

est_cattle_jobber.text: Off to the mart in Limerick. Grand city. King John's Castle, the Treaty Stone, and the best rugby supporters on God's earth. Ask them.
Don't ask them in the middle of a match, mind.
